title: Follow that man
told: an old story about Zeno and Crates

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? what’s the most embarrassing thing that’s happened to you in public?
options: everyone has one. watch what happens to zeno.
fair. zeno would rather not have, either.
lucky. this story will lend you one.

steps.line: Zeno looked up from the book about Socrates and asked the bookseller: where can I find people like this, today?

steps.q: Zeno asks where to find people like Socrates today. Right then, the bookseller points at a man walking past. Who do you think he is?
o: A Cynic who gave his fortune away
A general back from the wars
steps.why: Crates of Thebes. Diogenes Laërtius says he turned his estate into money and handed it out to his fellow citizens, to live free as a Cynic.

steps.line: Right then, a strange figure walked past the door. The bookseller pointed: “Follow that man.”
It was Crates, a Cynic philosopher. Born rich, he had given it all away, and said exactly what he thought. Zeno followed him.
But Zeno was shy. So Crates handed him a pot of lentil soup and told him to carry it through a busy part of Athens.

steps.q: Zeno tries to hide the pot under his cloak. What does Crates do?
o: Cracks the pot with his staff
steps.why: He broke it with his staff, right there in the street. Crates wanted the soup, and the shame, out in the open.

steps.line: Zeno hid it under his cloak. Crates cracked the pot with his staff. Soup ran down Zeno’s legs, and he ran.
Crates called after him: “Why run away, my little Phoenician? Nothing terrible has happened to you.”

steps.q: What was Crates teaching Zeno with the soup?
o: That a philosopher should own nothing, not even a pot
That he should never hide anything from his teacher
steps.why: Red face, wet legs, staring people. Embarrassing, yes. Harmful, no.

steps.q: Zeno later taught under a painted porch in Athens, and his students were named after it. What do we call them?
steps.why: Stoa poikile, the painted porch. Stoics like Seneca and Marcus Aurelius kept Crates’s lesson: only doing wrong is truly bad.

steps.line: Today: coffee down your shirt on a full train. Everyone looks. Spilled soup is only spilled soup.
steps.label: today

o: Families let him in to give advice
He broke into rich houses to shame them
He kept his own door open to beggars
steps.why: Diogenes Laërtius says he walked into any house and gave advice, and people welcomed it. Later writers say families asked him in to settle quarrels.

say: here’s what i love. look how it began: a curious question, a stranger walking past, and the nerve to get up and follow.

people called crates the door-opener, because families gladly let him in for advice. what he taught zeno, the stoics kept forever: embarrassment isn’t harm. be ashamed only of doing wrong. spilled soup isn’t wrong. it’s just soup.

steps.q: Why would a teacher pick something as small as soup, not a big test, for a shy student?
o: Cynics ate lentil soup every day
He wanted to see if Zeno would obey
You practice courage on small things
steps.why: Start small. If spilled soup can’t rule you, bigger things have less of a grip too.

today.say: today, when a small embarrassment comes, a wrong name, a spill, a typo in the group chat, say crates’s line to yourself: nothing terrible has happened to you. then carry on.
options: good. spilled soup is only spilled soup.
then you’ve already practiced. well done.

tomorrow.title: The painted porch.
tomorrow.line: no private school for zeno. he teaches out in the open, by the marketplace.

card.from: an old story about Zeno and Crates
sources: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 7.2–3 (R. D. Hicks, 1925): Zeno asks where men like Socrates are to be found; Crates passes by; the bookseller says, “Follow yonder man”; Zeno becomes his pupil but is too modest for Cynic shamelessness; Crates gives him a pot of lentil soup to carry through the Ceramicus; seeing him ashamed and trying to hide it, Crates breaks the pot with his staff; as Zeno runs off with the soup running down his legs, Crates says, “Why run away, my little Phoenician? nothing terrible has befallen you.”
Diogenes Laërtius 6.85–93 (Crates): born rich in Thebes, gave his property away; called the “Door-opener” because he entered every house and gave advice (6.86).
Teach: “be ashamed only of doing wrong” sums up the Stoic view that only vice is bad and only it deserves shame (DL 7.101–102; cf. Plutarch, Cato the Younger 6.3).
